Restored and annotated editions

The Science of Getting Rich

Wallace D. Wattles

Three men, a hundred and fifty years, one argument.

Read more

In 1758 a Philadelphia printer gathered twenty five years of his own proverbs into a single speech and gave it to an invented old man to deliver. In the 1870s a Baptist minister began telling a story about a farmer who sold his land to hunt for diamonds, and told it more than six thousand times to put poor students through the university he founded. In 1910 a midwestern writer published a short book claiming that wealth follows a law as reliable as gravity, died the year after, and was forgotten for most of a century until The Secret named him as its inspiration.

They are rarely bound together. They should be. The second is unthinkable without the first, and the third is unthinkable without the second. This edition prints them in reverse order of composition, so that reading it walks the doctrine back to its source.

The Science of Getting Rich (1910), Wallace D. Wattles, complete in all seventeen chapters

Acres of Diamonds, Russell H. Conwell, the lecture itself and not the biography usually bound with it

The Way to Wealth (1758), Benjamin Franklin, the work proper without the Victorian front matter

This annotated edition adds:

An original introduction tracing the lineage from Franklin through Conwell to Wattles, and naming plainly where Conwell's argument turns

A headnote before each of the three works

A glossary of the terms, people and places that have gone dark since

Dost thou love life? Then do not squander time, for that is the stuff life is made of.

What this edition adds

  • Wattles with Conwell's Acres of Diamonds and Franklin's The Way to Wealth
  • An Introduction tracing the line from Franklin to Wattles
  • A headnote for each work and a glossary of terms, people and places
